extracted.intended_audience: amateur and professional astronomers; scientifically literate public interested in Mars
extracted.subtask_description: Use telescopic observations (disk markings, polar caps, seasonal changes, limb-light, albedo, clouds, and detailed line features) to infer the presence of atmosphere, water, vegetation, and other planetary conditions on Mars; includes guidance on observing and characterizing the so-called canals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (1) — Rotation period
rubrics_metrics.description: Mars turns on its axis in 24 h. 37 m. 22.65 s. with reference to the stars, and in 24 h. 39 m. 35.0 s. (as a mean) with regard to the Sun. Its day, therefore, is only about forty minutes longer than ours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the summary list of empirical facts; used as evidence that Mars has a day length similar to Earth's, relevant to habitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (2) — Axial tilt
rubrics_metrics.description: Its axis is tilted to the plane of its orbit by about 23° 59′ (most recent determination, 1905). This gives the planet seasons almost the counterpart of our own in character; but in length nearly double ours, for
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axial tilt implies seasonality comparable to Earth, used as part of the ensemble of evidence for habitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (3) — Year length
rubrics_metrics.description: Its year consists of 687 of our days, 669 of its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual physical parameter; relevant to season length and climatic cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (4) — Visible polar caps that melt seasonally
rubrics_metrics.description: Polar caps are plainly visible which melt in the Martian summer to form again in the Martian winter, thus implying the presence of a substance deposited by cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal melting of caps is strong evidence for a volatile (likely water) component and seasonal climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (5) — Blue bordering belt excludes CO2 caps; indicates water
rubrics_metrics.description: As the polar caps melt, they are bordered by a blue belt, which retreats with them. This excludes the possibility of their being formed of carbon dioxide, and shows that of all the substances we know the material composing them must be water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific diagnostic: presence of a blue belt during melting used to distinguish water ice from CO2 ice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (6) — Southern cap blue-belt widenings correlate with blue-green areas
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of the southern cap, the blue belt has widenings in it in places. These occur where the blue-green areas bordering upon the polar cap are largest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spatial correlation between polar behavior and adjacent blue-green regions; supports connected hydrological/seasonal interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (7) — Polar caps' extensive shrinkage implies small quantity of ice
rubrics_metrics.description: The extensive shrinkage of the polar snows shows their quantity to be inconsiderable, and points to scanty deposition due to dearth of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to infer overall scarcity of water on the planet despite presence of seasonal ice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (8) — Melting occurs locally in a repeatable order (south cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: The melting takes place locally after the same general order and method, Martian year after year, both in the south cap,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated local melting pattern indicates predictable seasonal processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (9) — Melting occurs locally in a repeatable order (north cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: And in the north one. This is evidenced by the recurrence of rifts in the same places annually in each. The water thus let loose can, therefore, be locally counted on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual recurrence of rifts provides reliable seasonal signal and local water release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (10) — Southern cap shows greater extremes implying light deposition in both caps
rubrics_metrics.description: That the south polar cap is given to greater extremes than the north one, implies again, in view of the eccentricity of the orbit and the tilt of the axis, that deposition in both caps is light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymmetric cap behavior used to infer low total deposition of volatiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (11) — Temporary polar seas are fresh water
rubrics_metrics.description: The polar seas at the edges of the caps being temporary affairs, the water from them must be fresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If polar meltwater forms ephemeral seas, they are inferred to be fresh rather than saline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (12) — Melting and reforming caps prove water vapor in atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The melting of the caps on the one hand and their reforming on the other affirm the presence of water vapor in the Martian atmosphere, of whatever else that air consist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of atmospheric water vapor is inferred from seasonal cap dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (13) — Presence of water vapor implies heavier gases (N2, O2, CO2) probably present
rubrics_metrics.description: Since water vapor is present, of which the molecular weight is 18, it follows from the kinetic theory of gases that nitrogen, oxygen, and carbonic acid, of molecular weights 28, 32, and 38 respectively, are probably there, too, owing to being heavier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from kinetic theory used to infer likely presence of heavier gases if water vapor remains; an inferential criterion rather than direct detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (14) — Limb-light as evidence of atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The limb-light bears testimony to this atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optical limb phenomena are diagnostic of an atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (15) — Low albedo points to a very tenuous atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The planet’s low albedo points to a density for the atmosphere very much less than our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Albedo used as a proxy for atmospheric density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (16) — Apparent twilight supports tenuous atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent evidence of a twilight goes to confirm this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of twilight-like effects corroborates presence of a thin atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (17) — Permanent markings show surface is visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent markings show upon the disk, proving that the surface itself is visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent surface detail argues that atmosphere is not opaque; enables surface-based inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (18) — Disk divided into red-ochre and blue-green regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside of the polar cap the disk is divided into red-ochre and blue-green regions. The red-ochre stretches have the same appearance as our deserts seen from afar,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color-based regional mapping used to draw analogies with terrestrial surface types (deserts vs vegetated areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (19) — Red-ochre stretches behave like deserts (little affected by change)
rubrics_metrics.description: And behave as such, being but little affected by change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability of the ochre regions supports desert interpretation and scarcity of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (20) — Blue-green areas cannot be seas because they change with season and without compensating darkening elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: The blue-green areas were once thought to be seas. But they cannot be such, because they change in tint according to the Martian season, and the area and amount of the lightening is not offset at the time by corresponding darkening elsewhere;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal color changes inconsistent with liquid water bodies; used to rule out seas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (21) — Changes are not caused by shift of substance (no offsetting elsewhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor by any augmentation of the other polar cap or precipitation into cloud. It cannot, therefore, be due to shift of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminates simple redistribution of material as cause of color change; supports biological/vegetative interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (22) — Blue-green areas are seamed by permanent dark lines/spots, so no bodies of water
rubrics_metrics.description: Furthermore, they are all seamed by lines and spots darker than themselves which are permanent in place; so that there can be no bodies of water on the planet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of permanent seams contradicts fluid bodies and indicates surface features that persist through seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (23) — Blue-green color is that of vegetation and fades to ochre
rubrics_metrics.description: On the other hand, their color, blue-green, is that of vegetation; this regularly fades out, as vegetation would, to ochre for the most part, but in places changes to a chocolate-brown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color behavior analogized to terrestrial vegetation seasonal cycles; used as evidence for plant life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (24) — Change is seasonal in period as vegetation would be
rubrics_metrics.description: The change that comes over them is seasonal in period, as that of vegetation would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonality of changes supports biological interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (25) — Each hemisphere undergoes metamorphosis in turn
rubrics_metrics.description: Each hemisphere undergoes this metamorphosis in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposed-season behavior between hemispheres consistent with axial tilt-driven seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (26) — Recurrence is proof positive of an atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: That it is recurrent is again proof positive of an atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrent seasonal cycles require atmospheric mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (27) — Changes are metabolic (anabolic and katabolic), indicating vegetal origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The changes are metabolic, since those in one direction are later reversed to a restoration of the original status. Anabolic as well as katabolic processes thus go on there; that is, growth as well as decay takes place. This proves them of vegetal origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversibility of changes (growth and decay) used as a key criterion distinguishing organic processes from purely physical ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (28) — Existence of vegetation implies CO2, O2, N2 present
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of vegetation shows that carbonic acid, oxygen, and undoubtedly nitrogen, are present in the Martian atmosphere, since plants give out oxygen and take in carbonic acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biological presence used to infer atmospheric composition via terrestrial plant physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (29) — Dark-area changes follow polar-cap melting (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The changes in the dark areas follow upon the melting of the polar caps, not occurring until after that melting is under way;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal sequence (polar melt then area change) used to link seasonal water availability to surface metamorphosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (30) — Changes do not occur immediately after melt but after a lapse of time
rubrics_metrics.description: And not immediately then, but only after the lapse of a certain time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lag between melt and surface response consistent with growth/biological response times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (31) — Dark areas suggest old sea bottoms and appear as depressions on terminator
rubrics_metrics.description: Though not seas now, from their look the dark areas suggest old sea bottoms, and when on the terminator appear as depressions (whether because really at a lower level or because of less illumination is not certain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphological inference linking present dark areas to former basins favorable to vegetation in presence of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (32) — Dark areas now support vegetation, hinting at past aquatic role
rubrics_metrics.description: That they are now the parts of the planet to support vegetation hints the same past office, as water would naturally drain into them. That such a metamorphosis should occur with planetary aging is in keeping with the kinetic theory of gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines behavior, morphology, and theory to infer historical hydrology and planetary evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (33) — Terminator observations show no mountains; surface is surprisingly flat
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminator observations prove conclusively that there are no mountains on Mars, but that the surface is surprisingly flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface relief (or lack thereof) deduced from terminator profile; affects climate and drainage interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (34) — Clouds visible, often dust-storms
rubrics_metrics.description: But they do reveal clouds which are usually rare and are often, if not always, dust-storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transient atmospheric phenomena (clouds/dust) are part of the atmospheric evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (35) — White spots visible lasting weeks in tropic/temperate regions, indicating cold climate
rubrics_metrics.description: White spots are occasionally visible, lasting unchanged for weeks, in the tropic and temperate regions, showing that the climate is apparently cold,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent white spots are indicators of cold microclimates or frost; used to constrain temperature regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (36) — Most of surface temperature above freezing-point
rubrics_metrics.description: But at the same time proving that most of the surface has a temperature above the freezing-point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature inference balancing cold spots and general conditions; relevant to habitability potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (37) — Winter temperate zones covered by whitish veil (frost or cloud)
rubrics_metrics.description: In winter the temperate zones are more or less covered by a whitish veil, which may be hoar-frost or may be cloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal veiling indicates condensed volatiles; uncertain composition but diagnostic of climate cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (38) — Spring haze around north polar cap following melting
rubrics_metrics.description: A spring haze surrounds the north polar cap during the weeks that follow its most extensive melting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Haze occurrence tied to polar melting supports atmospheric transport of volatiles/humidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (39) — Otherwise Martian sky is perfectly clear like a dry desert land
rubrics_metrics.description: Otherwise the Martian sky is perfectly clear; like that of a dry and desert land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall clarity consistent with aridity and thin atmosphere; situates seasonal phenomena against a dry baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble-evidence principle for habitability
rubrics_metrics.description: If several pieces of evidence, distinct in their origin, concur to a given conclusion, the probability that that conclusion is correct is far greater than what results from each alone; and mounts up soon to something much exceeding what bettors at races call certainty odds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rubric: treat co-occurrence of independent lines of evidence (e.g., the 39 facts) as multiplicative support for the conclusion that Mars is habitable; supports using probabilistic synthesis rather than single-piece proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion criteria for habitability (summary list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering, now, these counts, we see that they make reasonably evident on Mars the presence of: 1. Days and seasons substantially like our own; 2. An atmosphere containing water vapor, carbonic acid, and oxygen; 3. Water in great scarcity; 4. A temperature colder than ours, but above the Fahrenheit freezing-point, except in winter and in the extreme polar regions; 5. Vegetation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five aggregated inferences form the author's formal conclusion criteria for declaring Mars 'habitable' — they synthesize the numbered facts into concrete inference targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere inference rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of air is attested first and foremost by the fact of change in the Martian markings (12), (13), (26), (28), and (35). The changes observed are conspicuous; are both inorganic (in the case of the polar caps), (12), (13), and (35), and metabolic or organic, (26) and (28). Such changes could not occur in the absence of an atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple, independent observed changes (polar cap dynamics, seasonal recurrence, metabolic-like changes, white spots) as combined evidence that an atmosphere exists and contains volatiles necessary for life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric composition inference via molecular-weight argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of water vapor (molecular weight 18) implies, from kinetic theory, that heavier gases like nitrogen, oxygen, and carbonic acid are probably present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theoretical inference rather than direct observation; include this as an interpretive criterion when water vapor is independently established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-scarcity inference rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: The extensive melting of the caps, the aspect and behavior of the reddish-ochre regions (deserts), and the detection that the blue-green areas are not seas (presence of permanent dark seams) all assert their non-aquatic constitution. No bodies of water are seen outside ephemeral polar seas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple lines (cap volume, desert-like expanses, permanent seams) together used to infer overall scarcity of surface water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation inference rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence for vegetation consists of static testimony from the look of the blue-green areas and kinematic derived from their behavior: seasonal, reversible (anabolic and katabolic) changes, color shifts from blue-green to ochre and to chocolate-brown in places, and timing correlated with polar-cap melt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine morphology (color), seasonality, reversibility, timing with meltwater, and spatial patterns to infer vegetal origin; requires ruling out all known inorganic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal detection — observer prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: When a fairly acute eyed observer sets himself to scan the telescopic disk of the planet in steady air, he will, after noting the main features, at times perceive thread-like features; persistence, an acute eye, and watching for the best moments in the steadiest air are required to perceive them reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: successful detection depends on observer acuity and persistence; not every observer will see canals without training and favorable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal detection — ephemeral appearance and need for repeated observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The lines may appear suddenly and vanish; after three or four showings repetition in situ convinces the observer they are real. Persistence increases frequency and detail of appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: require repeated sightings in the same place (in situ repetition) before accepting fleeting features as genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal detection — atmospheric steadiness critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmospheric conditions far superior to what are good enough for most astronomic observations are needed; poor air spreads delicate features into diffuse streaks and can mask the true fine-line nature of the canals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measurement criterion: only accept fine linear details when observed under superior seeing; otherwise treat streaks as potentially artifactual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal morphology — lines (one-dimensional) not two-dimensional features
rubrics_metrics.description: The canals are lines in the precise geometric sense; they are distinct from main two-dimensional markings (which have extension in two dimensions); these canals have extension mainly in one dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive criterion for classification: if a marking behaves as a geometrically straight, uniform-width line across the disk it belongs to the canal class rather than the main-region class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal morphology — straightness and geometric regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The lines run straight throughout their course. Ninety percent are absolutely straight and the remaining ten percent curve in symmetric manner; they look 'laid down by rule and compass'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high straightness and geometric regularity as diagnostic features distinguishing canals from natural irregular markings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal morphology — uniform width
rubrics_metrics.description: Equally striking is the uniform width of each line from its beginning to its end; the line varies not in size throughout its course any more than it deviates in direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform width throughout a feature's length is a key morphological diagnostic of canals when resolved under good seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canals are peculiar to Mars (no terrestrial analogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the main markings bear a family resemblance to those of the Earth, the canals are peculiar to Mars, finding no counterpart upon the earth at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat canals as a distinct Martian phenomenon; lack of earthly analogue cautions against terrestrial-based explanatory models without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal naming caveat — not to be taken as literal dug canals
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful as the name 'canal' is, it must not be supposed that what we see are such in any simple sense. No observer has considered them canals dug like the Suez or Panama ones; that supposition is of critic creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology warning: avoid literal engineering interpretations of optical linear markings without corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal width measurement — only an outside limit is determinable
rubrics_metrics.description: Their precise width is not precisable. They show no measurable breadth and their size admits only of an outside limit. The sole method of estimating their width is by comparison of effect with a wire of known caliber at a known distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement protocol: rely on comparison experiments (e.g., wire subtension) to set upper bounds on apparent width; avoid claiming precise absolute widths from telescopic appearance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal visual broadening is atmospheric seeing artifact
rubrics_metrics.description: Air waves spread very slender markings into diffuse streaks; as seeing improves, apparent breadth contracts. Agitations in Earth's air broaden the lines more than other features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation rule: treat observed breadth/blur of canals as a function of seeing quality; improvements in seeing should make canals appear finer rather than broader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation verification protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Success depends upon the acuteness of the observer’s eye and the persistence with which he watches for the best moments in the steadiest air. Under excellent conditions the tapestry-like reticulation of lines becomes unambiguously evident and permanent in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification requires (a) multiple observers where possible, (b) repeated observations in steady air, and (c) documentation of persistent in situ positions before treating features as real.
